title: The Thinkery and the Lyceum: the Clouds and the Peripatetic corpus — a groundwork note on relations, withholding readings (v1.0)
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: The Clouds of Aristophanes and the treatises under the names Aristotle and Theophrastus share a curriculum. This groundwork note, in the manner of Catalogues and Wills (#1581) and Two Lists of Stones (#1592), sets the two side by side, locus by locus in the seated Greek: the things aloft and under the earth, thought carried in dry air against moisture (ἰκμάς), thunder and the thunderbolt as enclosed dry wind, sound driven by breath through a narrow passage, the weaker argument, the genders of nouns, the Vortex in place of Zeus, and the rustic pupil, with the predecessor to whom the treatises assign each. It then sets the charge apparatus side by side: the comedy's research called μυστήρια and its first joke ending on escaping a suit; the King Archon of the Constitution of the Athenians 57, who holds the Mysteries, the Lenaean contest and the indictments for impiety; the Euthyphro's Socrates walking from the Lyceum to the King's Stoa; the Apology's naming of Aristophanes' comedy and the Crito's refused flight; and Diogenes Laertius on Aristotle's withdrawal to Chalcis under an impiety charge brought by the hierophant Eurymedon, a name that also stands in Plato's will and in the family of Speusippus. No dependence is asserted, no chronology argued and no author proposed.

methodology: Read the Clouds by the edition's line numbers with its speaker markup; locate each subject of the thinkery's curriculum in the seated treatises and record to whom the treatises assign it; set the charge apparatus (the Mysteries, the comic contest, the impiety indictment, the Lyceum) across the comedy, the Constitution of the Athenians, the dialogues and Diogenes Laertius; tabulate both; state what is not claimed.
falsification_conditions: Falsified if a quoted locus does not stand in the seated text at the place given; if a line is given to the wrong speaker; if a subject the note tabulates as shared is absent from one side; if a treatise's assignment of a doctrine to a predecessor is misreported; or if the note asserts a dependence, a chronology or an authorship it says it withholds.

wiki_article: The Thinkery and the Lyceum is a groundwork note by Lee Sharks, published in Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology and deposited on 20 November 2026. It sets the Clouds of Aristophanes beside the treatises under the names Aristotle and Theophrastus and records the relations without readings. Its first part tabulates one curriculum in two registers: the things aloft and under the earth (Clouds 188, 194, 228; Meteorologica I 1; Apology 19b, 23d), thought in dry air against moisture, ἰκμάς (Clouds 228–233; Theophrastus, De sensibus, reporting Diogenes of Apollonia), thunder and the thunderbolt (Clouds 386–411; Meteorologica II 9), sound driven by breath through a narrow passage (the gnat, Clouds 156–164; Historia animalium IV 9), the weaker argument (Clouds 112–115, 1038–1042; Rhetoric II 24, given to Protagoras), the genders of nouns (Clouds 658–680; Rhetoric III 5 and Sophistical Refutations 14, given to Protagoras), the Vortex (Clouds 379–380, 828, 1471; De caelo II 13) and the rustic (Clouds 43, 628, 646; Characters 4). Its second part sets the charge apparatus side by side: the comedy's research called mysteries and its escape from a suit; the King Archon of the Constitution of the Athenians 57, who holds the Mysteries, the Lenaean contest and the indictments for impiety; the Euthyphro's Socrates leaving the Lyceum for the King's Stoa; the Apology's naming of Aristophanes' comedy; the Crito's refused flight; and Diogenes Laertius on Aristotle's withdrawal to Chalcis under an impiety charge by the hierophant Eurymedon, a name that also stands in Plato's will and in the family of Speusippus. The note asserts no dependence, chronology or authorship.

defines_concepts.definition: In The Thinkery and the Lyceum, the relation set down between the Clouds and the Peripatetic treatises: the same subjects of study, several in the same words, held once as comedy and once as treatise, with the treatises naming predecessors for most of them.
